prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center on the afternoon of April 11, 1970, and for its first two days it seemed the most routine flight in the program. It was NASA's third attempt to land men on the Moon, and the public, having watched two successful landings already, had grown a little bored with the whole enterprise. The crew consisted of Jim Lovell, a veteran of four spaceflights who was about to become the first person to travel to the Moon twice, along with Fred Haise, a rookie who would pilot the lunar module, and Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been grounded after exposure to German measles, and Swigert stepped in with barely any time to prepare. The spacecraft itself was made of two parts, a command module the crew called Odyssey and a spidery lunar module named Aquarius, which was meant to carry Lovell and Haise to the surface of the Moon.

On the evening of April 13, about fifty-six hours into the flight and roughly 200,000 miles from Earth, controllers in Houston asked the crew to stir the cryogenic tanks in the service module, the cylindrical section behind the command module that held their oxygen, hydrogen, and much of their electrical machinery. The stirring was a routine chore meant to keep the supercold contents from stratifying. Swigert flipped the switch, and a few moments later there was a bang and a shudder that the astronauts felt through the whole ship. Swigert reported that they had a problem, and Lovell, asked to repeat the message, said it again. Warning lights lit up across the panel, and the voltage on the main electrical buses began to sag.

The cause, discovered only later, lay in events that predated the launch by years. Oxygen tank number two had been dropped slightly during handling at the factory, and during ground testing its heaters had run far hotter than intended, baking away the insulation on the wires inside. When Swigert threw the switch, a spark in the damaged tank ignited the insulation in an atmosphere of pure oxygen, and the resulting pressure burst the tank and blew a panel off the side of the service module. The second oxygen tank was crippled too, and within hours it had drained away into space. Without oxygen the fuel cells that supplied the command module's power and water would soon die, and Lovell, peering out a window, saw the gas venting into the void and understood that the Moon landing was over.

Mission Control now faced a different question, which was how to keep three men alive. The command module would need its small reserve of battery power to survive the fiery return through the atmosphere, so it had to be shut down almost completely and saved. The only available refuge was the lunar module, a craft designed to support two men for about two days on the Moon, and now expected to sustain three men for four days. The crew moved into Aquarius and began using it as a lifeboat, a possibility that engineers had considered on paper but never really practiced. Flight director Gene Kranz and his teams of controllers worked in shifts around the clock, and hundreds of engineers across the country joined them to improvise the procedures that would be needed.

The next decision concerned the route home. The spacecraft had been placed on a path that would carry it around the Moon and, had nothing been done, would swing it back toward Earth, though not close enough to survive. Controllers could try to turn the ship around at once, but that required using the damaged service module's main engine, whose condition was unknown. They chose instead to loop around the far side of the Moon and fire the lunar module's descent engine after passing it, a burn that shortened the trip and aimed the ship at the Pacific Ocean. The maneuver worked well. Along the way Apollo 13 passed about 100 miles beyond the Moon's far side, and at the greatest point of its journey it carried the three men nearly 250,000 miles from Earth, farther than any human beings had ever traveled.

Surviving the long return proved almost as difficult as the explosion. The lunar module's air was being scrubbed of carbon dioxide by canisters of lithium hydroxide, and these were soon saturated. Spare canisters existed in the command module, but they were square and the lunar module's receptacles were round. On the ground, engineers gathered the same materials the crew had aboard, including plastic bags, cardboard, suit hoses, and duct tape, and assembled a crude adapter that would let the square canisters work. They read the instructions to the astronauts over the radio, step by step, and the crew built the device and watched the carbon dioxide levels fall. Meanwhile the cabin grew bitterly cold as the systems were powered down, dropping to near freezing, and the men slept little. Water was rationed to a few ounces per day, and Haise developed a fever from a kidney infection while Lovell, Swigert, and he lost many pounds between them.

Navigation also demanded invention. With the ship's computer and guidance platform shut off, the crew had to align the craft by hand, and at one point they used the sun, and at another the terminator line of the Earth, as reference points. They carried out several small course corrections by manual control, and any error in them could have left the ship skipping off the atmosphere or burning up in it. Back in Houston, Mattingly, who had never caught the measles after all, spent long hours in a simulator working out how to bring the command module back to life using as little power as possible. His procedure, a delicate sequence of switches that stayed within the strict limits of the batteries, was read up to the crew in the last day of the flight.

As the spacecraft closed on Earth on April 17, the crew first discarded the damaged service module, and when it floated away they saw for the first time how badly it had been wrecked, with an entire side missing and ruined equipment trailing out of it. They then powered up Odyssey and, last of all, released Aquarius, which had carried them so faithfully. Reentry brought the expected communications blackout, normally about three minutes long, and in Houston the controllers waited in silence as the minutes stretched on. At last, after nearly a minute more than anyone expected, Swigert's voice came through, and in the control room the tension broke. Three parachutes opened above the capsule, and at about noon, Houston time, Odyssey settled into the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The flight had lasted almost six days.

A review board led by Edgar Cortright traced the accident to the faulty tank and its wiring, and NASA redesigned the oxygen system before flying again. The agency later landed crews on the Moon on Apollo 14 and on subsequent missions, though public interest in the program continued to fade. Lovell never walked on the Moon, but the ordeal made him and his crew, along with the controllers on the ground, symbols of what disciplined people can do under pressure. President Nixon awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom to the mission operations team, and Apollo 13 is still remembered, with a certain irony, as NASA's most successful failure.
